procedural_history.originating_court: Bombay High Court and Calcutta High Court
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgments and orders of the Bombay High Court dated November 9, 1967 (in Criminal Revision Application No. 475 of 1967 and Criminal Revision Application No. 447 of 1967) and November 14, 1967 (in Criminal Revision Application No. 682 of 1967) and the Calcutta High Court dated September 8, 1966 (in Criminal Revision No. 231 of 1965)
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Bombay High Court heard Criminal Revision Application Nos. 475, 447 and 682 of 1967. The Calcutta High Court heard Criminal Revision No. 231 of 1965. The High Court rejected the petitions.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached via appeals by special leave from the judgments and orders of the Bombay and Calcutta High Courts. The cases before the Supreme Court are Criminal Appeal No. 27 of 1967, Criminal Appeal Nos. 45, 46 and 47 of 1968.

issue.issue_text: Whether the admissibility of a statement made to a Customs Officer under the Sea Customs Act, 1878, in a subsequent trial, must be judged in light of the law existing at the time of the trial, especially after the repeal of the said Act.

facts: A statement was made to a Customs Officer during an inquiry under the Sea Customs Act, 1878.
Subsequently, the Sea Customs Act, 1878, was repealed and replaced by the Customs Act, 1962.
At a trial that took place after the repeal, the prosecution sought to admit the statement into evidence.
The accused argued that the admissibility of the statement should be judged under the new law (the Customs Act, 1962) which was in force at the time of the trial.
law: The admissibility of a statement made under a specific statute must be judged based on the legal conditions and any potential "taint" (such as inadmissibility) that attached to it at the time it was made.
The subsequent repeal of the statute under which the statement was recorded does not change the criteria for determining its admissibility.
application: The Court applied the principle that the legal status of the statement was fixed when it was made under the Sea Customs Act, 1878.
It held that even though the Act was later repealed, the question of admissibility still depended on whether the statement was tainted when it was originally made.
The Court specified that this determination would depend on the application of Section 25 of the Evidence Act and Article 20(3) of the Constitution to the statement at the time it was given.
Therefore, the argument that the new Act of 1962 should govern the admissibility of a statement made under the old Act was dismissed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention, ruling that the admissibility of the statement must be judged in light of the law and any taint attaching to it at the time the statement was made, not by the law in force at the time of the trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the admissibility of a statement made to a Customs Officer under the Sea Customs Act, 1878, in a subsequent trial, must be judged in light of the law existing at the time of the trial, especially after the repeal of the said Act.
appellant_arguments: The statements tendered in evidence by the Customs Officer must be deemed by virtue of s. 160 of the Customs Act 52 of 1962 to be recorded under the provisions of that Act.
Consequently, the admissibility of these statements should be adjudged in the light of the Customs Act, 1962, alone, which was the law in force at the time of the trial.
respondent_arguments: Even after the repeal of the Sea Customs Act, the admissibility of a statement made for a contravention of that Act must be judged in light of the law existing when the statement was made.
The admissibility must be determined by the 'taint', if any, that attached to the statement at the time it was made, not by the law at the time of the trial.

cases.case_name: Laxman Padma Bhagat v. The State
cases.principle: A person examined under s. 171-A of the Sea Customs Act, 1878, does not stand in the character of an accused person because there is no formal accusation made against him at that time.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Actions, such as notifications, rules, orders, or appointments, taken under a repealed enactment are deemed to have been done under the corresponding provision of the new Act, so long as they are not inconsistent with the new Act's provisions.
obiter: The powers that police officers enjoy are for the effective prevention and detection of crime in order to maintain law and order.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The contention that a person against whom an enquiry is made by a Customs Officer under the Sea Customs Act is a person accused of an offence, and that evidence collected by examining him is inadmissible, has no substance. The protection of Article 20(3) of the Constitution is not triggered because an inquiry by a Customs Officer does not amount to a 'formal accusation' against the person. Furthermore, a Customs Officer is not a police officer, as they are not entrusted with the duty to maintain law and order, so a statement made to them is not barred by Section 25 of the Evidence Act.
legal_tests_applied: To invoke the constitutional guarantee against self-incrimination under Article 20(3), an essential condition is that a 'formal accusation relating to the commission of an offence, which would normally lead to his prosecution, must have been levelled against the party'.

Whether an officer is a 'police-officer' for the purposes of the Evidence Act depends on their primary duties; police officers are those who have powers for the 'effective prevention and detection of crime in order to maintain law and order'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that an inquiry under the Sea Customs Act makes a person 'accused of an offence' was rejected, as the court held this did not meet the 'formal accusation' test required to activate Article 20(3) protection.

The court found that a Customs Officer is not a member of the police force and is not entrusted with the duty to maintain law and order, therefore a confession made to such an officer is not inadmissible under Section 25 of the Evidence Act.

The court explicitly overruled the view from the Calcutta High Court that a proceeding under s. 171-A of the Sea Customs Act was a formal accusation, stating that such a view is inconsistent with Supreme Court judgments and cannot be accepted as correct.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was affirmed because the court applied its precedent from *The State of Bombay v. Kathi Kalu Oghad*, which established that the protection of Article 20(3) is only available after a formal accusation has been made.

The court accepted the distinction between the duties of a Customs Officer and a police officer, thereby concluding that the bar on admissibility of confessions made to police officers does not apply to statements made to Customs Officers.

The admissibility of the statement was determined by the legal character of the inquiry at the time it was conducted under the Sea Customs Act, 1878, under which the person was not considered 'accused' and the officer was not considered 'police'.
policy_considerations: The court noted that the purpose of Section 25 of the Evidence Act, which declares confessions to police officers inadmissible, is 'to avoid the danger of admitting false confessional statements obtained by coercion, torture or ill-treatment.' By distinguishing Customs Officers from police, the court implies that this specific danger is not considered to be present in the same way during a customs inquiry.
